Having, therefore, received the seal, they had one understanding and one mind; and their faith became one, and their love one, and with the name they bore also the spirits of the virgins. On this account the building of the tower became of one colour, bright as the sun. But after they had entered into the same place, and became one body, certain of these defiled themselves, and were expelled from the race of the righteous, and became again what they were before, or rather worse.”

“How, sir,” I said, “did they become worse, after having known God?” “He that does not know God,” he answered, “and practises evil, receives a certain chastisement for his wickedness; but he that has known God, ought not any longer to do evil, but to do good. If, accordingly, when he ought to do good, he do evil, does not he appear to do greater evil than he who does not know God? For this reason, they who have not known God and do evil are condemned to death; but they who have known God, and have seen His mighty works, and still continue in evil, shall be chastised doubly, and shall die for ever. In this way, then, will the church of God be purified. For as you saw the stones rejected from the tower, and delivered to the evil spirits, and cast out thence, so [they also shall be cast out, and] there shall be one body of the purified, as the tower also became, as it were, of one stone after its purification. In like manner also shall it be with the church of God, after it has been purified, and has rejected the wicked, and the hypocrites, and the blasphemers, and the waverers, and those who commit wickedness of different kinds. After these have been cast away, the church of God shall be one body, of one mind, of one understanding, of one faith, of one love. And then the Son of God will be exceeding glad, and shall rejoice over them, because He has received His people pure.” “All these things, sir,” I said, “are great and glorious.

“Moreover, sir,” I said, “explain to me the power and the actions of each one of the mountains, that every soul, trusting in the Lord, and hearing it, may glorify His great, and marvellous, and glorious name.” “Hear,” he said, “the diversity of the mountains and of the twelve nations.”

“From the first mountain, which was black, they that believed are the following: apostates and blasphemers against the Lord, and betrayers of the servants of God. To these repentance is not open; but death lies before them, and on this account also are they black, for their race is a lawless one. And from the second mountain, which was bare, they who believed are the following: hypocrites, and teachers of wickedness. And these, accordingly, are like the former, not having any fruits of righteousness; for as their mountain was destitute of fruit, so also such men have a name indeed, but are empty of faith, and there is no fruit of truth in them. They indeed have repentance in their power, if they repent quickly; but if they are slow in so doing, they shall die along with the former.” “Why, sir,” I said, “have these repentance, but the former not? for their actions are nearly the same.” “On this account,” he said, “have these repentance, because they did not blaspheme their Lord, nor become betrayers of the servants of God; but on account of their desire of possessions they became hypocritical, and each one taught according to the desires of men that were sinners. But they will suffer a certain punishment; and repentance is before them, because they were not blasphemers or traitors.”

“And from the third mountain, which had thorns and thistles, they who believed are the following. There are some of them rich, and others immersed in much business. The thistles are the rich, and the thorns are they who are immersed in much business. Those, [accordingly, who are entangled in many various kinds of business, do not] cleave to the servants of God, but wander away, being choked by their business transactions; and the rich cleave with difficulty to the servants of God, fearing lest these should ask something of them. Such persons, accordingly, shall have difficulty in entering into the kingdom of God. For as it is disagreeable to walk among thistles with naked feet, so also it is hard for such to enter the kingdom of God. But to all these repentance, and that speedy, is open, in order that what they did not do in former times they may make up for in these days, and do some good, and they shall live unto God. But if they abide in their deeds, they shall be delivered to those women, who will put them to death.”

“And from the fourth mountain, which had much grass, the upper parts of the plants green, and the parts about the roots withered, and some also scorched by the sun, they who believed are the following: the doubtful, and they who have the Lord upon their lips, but have Him not in their heart. On this account their foundations are withered, and have no strength; and their words alone live, while their works are dead. Such persons are [neither alive nor] dead. They resemble, therefore, the waverers: for the wavering are neither withered nor green, being neither living nor dead. For as their blades, on seeing the sun, were withered, so also the wavering, when they hear of affliction, on account of their fear, worship idols, and are ashamed of the name of their Lord. Such, then, are neither alive nor dead. But these also may yet live, if they repent quickly; and if they do not repent, they are already delivered to the women, who take away their life.”

“And from the fifth mountain, which had green grass, and was rugged, they who believed are the following: believers, indeed, but slow to learn, and obstinate, and pleasing themselves, wishing to know everything, and knowing nothing at all. On account of this obstinacy of theirs, understanding departed from them, and foolish senselessness entered into them. And they praise themselves as having wisdom, and desire to become teachers, although destitute of sense. On account, therefore, of this loftiness of mind, many became vain, exalting themselves: for self-will and empty confidence is a great demon. Of these, accordingly, many were rejected, but some repented and believed, and subjected themselves to those that had understanding, knowing their own foolishness. And to the rest of this class repentance is open; for they were not wicked, but rather foolish, and without understanding. If these therefore repent, they will live unto God; but if they do not repent, they shall have their dwelling with the women who wrought wickedness among them.”

“And those from the sixth mountain, which had clefts large and small, and decayed grass in the clefts, who believed, were the following: they who occupy the small clefts are those who bring charges against one another, and by reason of their slanders have decayed in the faith. Many of them, however, repented; and the rest also will repent when they hear my commandments, for their slanders are small, and they will quickly repent. But they who occupy the large clefts are persistent in their slanders, and vindictive in their anger against each other. These, therefore, were thrown away from the tower, and rejected from having a part in its building. Such persons, accordingly, shall have difficulty in living. If our God and Lord, who rules over all things, and has power over all His creation, does not remember evil against those who confess their sins, but is merciful, does man, who is corruptible and full of sins, remember evil against a fellow-man, as if he were able to destroy or to save him? I, the angel of repentance, say unto you, As many of you as are of this way of thinking, lay it aside, and repent, and the Lord will heal your former sins, if you purify yourselves from this demon; but if not, you will be delivered over to him for death.”

“And those who believed from the seventh mountain, on which the grass was green and flourishing, and the whole of the mountain fertile, and every kind of cattle and the fowls of heaven were feeding on the grass on this mountain, and the grass on which they pastured became more abundant, were the following: they were always simple, and harmless, and blessed, bringing no charges against one another, but always rejoicing greatly because of the servants of God, and being clothed with the holy spirit of these virgins, and always having pity on every man, and giving aid from their own labour to every man, without reproach and without hesitation. The Lord, therefore, seeing their simplicity and all their meekness, multiplied them amid the labours of their hands, and gave them grace in all their doings. And I, the angel of repentance, say to you who are such, Continue to be such as these, and your seed will never be blotted out; for the Lord has made trial of you, and inscribed you in the number of us, and the whole of your seed will dwell with the Son of God; for ye have received of His Spirit.”

“And they who believed from the eighth mountain, where were the many fountains, and where all the creatures of God drank of the fountains, were the following: apostles, and teachers, who preached to the whole world, and who taught solemnly and purely the word of the Lord, and did not at all fall into evil desires, but walked always in righteousness and truth, according as they had received the Holy Spirit. Such persons, therefore, shall enter in with the angels.”

“And they who believed from the ninth mountain, which was deserted, and had in it creeping things and wild beasts which destroy men, were the following: they who had the stains are servants, who discharged their duty ill, and who plundered widows and orphans of their livelihood, and gained possessions for themselves from the ministry, which they had received. If, therefore, they remain under the dominion of the same desire, they are dead, and there is no hope of life for them; but if they repent, and finish their ministry in a holy manner, they shall be able to live. And they who were covered with scabs are those who have denied their Lord, and have not returned to Him again; but becoming withered and desert-like, and not cleaving to the servants of God, but living in solitude, they destroy their own souls. For as a vine, when left within an enclosure, and meeting with neglect, is destroyed, and is made desolate by the weeds, and in time grows wild, and is no longer of any use to its master, so also are such men as have given themselves up, and become useless to their Lord, from having contracted savage habits. These men, therefore, have repentance in their power, unless they are found to have denied from the heart; but if any one is found to have denied from the heart, I do not know if he may live. And I say this not for these present days, in order that any one who has denied may obtain repentance, for it is impossible for him to be saved who now intends to deny his Lord; but to those who denied Him long ago, repentance seems to be possible. If, therefore, any one intends to repent, let him do so quickly, before the tower is completed; for if not, he will be utterly destroyed by the women. And the chipped stones are the deceitful and the slanderers; and the wild beasts, which you saw on the ninth mountain, are the same. For as wild beasts destroy and kill a man by their poison, so also do the words of such men destroy and ruin a man. These, accordingly, are mutilated in their faith, on account of the deeds which they have done in themselves; yet some repented, and were saved. And the rest, who are of such a character, can be saved if they repent; but if they do not repent, they will perish with those women, whose strength they have assumed.”

“And from the tenth mountain, where were trees which overshadowed certain sheep, they who believed were the following: bishops given to hospitality, who always gladly received into their houses the servants of God, without dissimulation. And the bishops never failed to protect, by their service, the widows, and those who were in want, and always maintained a holy conversation. All these, accordingly, shall be protected by the Lord for ever. They who do these things are honourable before God, and their place is already with the angels, if they remain to the end serving God.”

“And from the eleventh mountain, where were trees full of fruits, adorned with fruits of various kinds, they who believed were the following: they who suffered for the name of the Son of God, and who also suffered cheerfully with their whole heart, and laid down their lives.” “Why, then, sir,” I said, “do all these trees bear fruit, and some of them fairer than the rest?” “Listen,” he said; “all who once suffered for the name of the Lord are honourable before God; and of all these the sins were remitted, because they suffered for the name of the Son of God. And why their fruits are of various kinds, and some of them superior, listen. All,” he continued, “who were brought before the authorities and were examined, and did not deny, but suffered cheerfully—these are held in greater honour with God, and of these the fruit is superior; but all who were cowards, and in doubt, and who reasoned in their hearts whether they would deny or confess, and yet suffered, of these the fruit is less, because that suggestion came into their hearts; for that suggestion—that a servant should deny his Lord—is evil. Have a care, therefore, ye who are planning such things, lest that suggestion remain in your hearts, and ye perish unto God. And ye who suffer for His name ought to glorify God, because He deemed you worthy to bear His name, that all your sins might be healed. [Therefore, rather deem yourselves happy], and think that ye have done a great thing, if any of you suffer on account of God. The Lord bestows upon you life, and ye do not understand, for your sins were heavy; but if you had not suffered for the name of the Lord, ye would have died to God on account of your sins. These things I say to you who are hesitating about denying or confessing: acknowledge that ye have the Lord, lest, denying Him, ye be delivered up to prison. If the heathen chastise their slaves, when one of them denies his master, what, think ye, will your Lord do, who has authority over all men? Put away these counsels out of your hearts, that you may live continually unto God.”

“And they who believed from the twelfth mountain, which was white, are the following: they are as infant children, in whose hearts no evil originates; nor did they know what wickedness is, but always remained as children. Such accordingly, without doubt, dwell in the kingdom of God, because they defiled in nothing the commandments of God; but they remained like children all the days of their life in the same mind. All of you, then, who shall remain stedfast, and be as children, without doing evil, will be more honoured than all who have been previously mentioned; for all infants are honourable before God, and are the first persons with Him. Blessed, then, are ye who put away wickedness from yourselves, and put on innocence. As the first of all will you live unto God.”

After he had finished the similitudes of the mountains, I said to him, “Sir, explain to me now about the stones that were taken out of the plain, and put into the building instead of the stones that were taken out of the tower; and about the round stones that were put into the building; and those that still remain round.”

“Hear,” he answered, “about all these also. The stones taken out of the plain and put into the building of the tower instead of those that were rejected, are the roots of this white mountain. When, therefore, they who believed from the white mountain were all found guileless, the Lord of the tower commanded those from the roots of this mountain to be cast into the building of the tower; for he knew that if these stones were to go to the building of the tower, they would remain bright, and not one of them become black. But if he had so resolved with respect to the other mountains, it would have been necessary for him to visit that tower again, and to cleanse it. Now all these persons were found white who believed, and who will yet believe, for they are of the same race. This is a happy race, because it is innocent. Hear now, further, about these round and shining stones. All these also are from the white mountain. Hear, moreover, why they were found round: because their riches had obscured and darkened them a little from the truth, although they never departed from God; nor did any evil word proceed out of their mouth, but all justice, virtue, and truth. When the Lord, therefore, saw the mind of these persons, that they were born good, and could be good, He ordered their riches to be cut down, not to be taken away for ever, that they might be able to do some good with what was left them; and they will live unto God, because they are of a good race. Therefore were they rounded a little by the chisel, and put in the building of the tower.”

“But the other round stones, which had not yet been adapted to the building of the tower, and had not yet received the seal, were for this reason put back into their place, because they are exceedingly round. Now this age must be cut down in these things, and in the vanities of their riches, and then they will meet in the kingdom of God; for they must of necessity enter into the kingdom of God, because the Lord has blessed this innocent race. Of this race, therefore, no one will perish; for although any of them be tempted by the most wicked devil, and commit sin, he will quickly return to his Lord. I deem you happy, I, who am the messenger of repentance, whoever of you are innocent as children, because your part is good, and honourable before God. Moreover, I say to you all, who have received the seal of the Son of God, be clothed with simplicity, and be not mindful of offences, nor remain in wickedness. Lay aside, therefore, the recollection of your offences and bitternesses, and you will be formed in one spirit. And heal and take away from you those wicked schisms, that if the Lord of the flocks come, He may rejoice concerning you. And He will rejoice, if He find all things sound, and none of you shall perish. But if He find any one of these sheep strayed, woe to the shepherds! And if the shepherds themselves have strayed, what answer will they give Him for their flocks? Will they perchance say that they were harassed by their flocks? They will not be believed, for the thing is incredible that a shepherd could suffer from his flock; rather will he be punished on account of his falsehood. And I myself am a shepherd, and I am under a most stringent necessity of rendering an account of you.”

“Heal yourselves, therefore, while the tower is still building. The Lord dwells in men that love peace, because He loved peace; but from the contentious and the utterly wicked He is far distant. Restore to Him, therefore, a spirit sound as ye received it. For when you have given to a fuller a new garment, and desire to receive it back entire at the end, if, then, the fuller return you a torn garment, will you take it from him, and not rather be angry, and abuse him, saying, ‘I gave you a garment that was entire: why have you rent it, and made it useless, so that it can be of no use on account of the rent which you have made in it?’ Would you not say all this to the fuller about the rent which you found in your garment? If, therefore, you grieve about your garment, and complain because you have not received it entire, what do you think the Lord will do to you, who gave you a sound spirit, which you have rendered altogether useless, so that it can be of no service to its possessor? for its use began to be unprofitable, seeing it was corrupted by you. Will not the Lord, therefore, because of this conduct of yours regarding His Spirit, act in the same way, and deliver you over to death? Assuredly, I say, he will do the same to all those whom He shall find retaining a recollection of offences. Do not trample His mercy under foot, He says, but rather honour Him, because He is so patient with your sins, and is not as ye are. Repent, for it is useful to you.”

“All these things which are written above, I, the Shepherd, the messenger of repentance, have showed and spoken to the servants of God. If therefore ye believe, and listen to my words, and walk in them, and amend your ways, you shall have it in your power to live: but if you remain in wickedness, and in the recollection of offences, no sinner of that class will live unto God. All these words which I had to say have been spoken unto you.”

The Shepherd said to me, “Have you asked me everything?” And I replied, “Yes, sir.” “Why did you not ask me about the shape of the stones that were put into the building, that I might explain to you why we filled up the shapes?” And I said, “I forgot, sir.” “Hear now, then,” he said, “about this also. These are they who have now heard my commandments, and repented with their whole hearts. And when the Lord saw that their repentance was good and pure, and that they were able to remain in it, He ordered their former sins to be blotted out. For these shapes were their sins, and they were levelled down, that they might not appear.”

After I had fully written down this book, that messenger who had delivered me to the Shepherd came into the house in which I was, and sat down upon a couch, and the Shepherd stood on his right hand. He then called me, and spoke to me as follows: “I have delivered you and your house to the Shepherd, that you may be protected by him.” “Yes, sir,” I said. “If you wish, therefore, to be protected,” he said, “from all annoyance, and from all harsh treatment, and to have success in every good work and word, and to possess all the virtues of righteousness, walk in these commandments which he has given you, and you will be able to subdue all wickedness. For if you keep those commandments, every desire and pleasure of the world will be subject to you, and success will attend you in every good work. Take unto yourself his experience and moderation, and say to all that he is in great honour and dignity with God, and that he is a president with great power, and mighty in his office. To him alone throughout the whole world is the power of repentance assigned. Does he seem to you to be powerful? But you despise his experience, and the moderation which he exercises towards you.”

I said to him, “Ask himself, sir, whether from the time that he has entered my house I have done anything improper, or have offended him in any respect.” He answered, “I also know that you neither have done nor will do anything improper, and therefore I speak these words to you, that you may persevere. For he had a good report of you to me, and you will say these words to others, that they also who have either repented or will still repent may entertain the same feelings with you, and he may report well of these to me, and I to the Lord.” And I said, “Sir, I make known to every man the great works of God: and I hope that all those who love them, and have sinned before, on hearing these words, may repent, and receive life again.” “Continue, therefore, in this ministry, and finish it. And all who follow out his commands shall have life, and great honour with the Lord. But those who do not keep his commandments, flee from his life, and despise him. But he has his own honour with the Lord. All, therefore, who shall despise him, and not follow his commands, deliver themselves to death, and every one of them will be guilty of his own blood. But I enjoin you, that you obey his commands, and you will have a cure for your former sins.”

“Moreover, I sent you these virgins, that they may dwell with you. For I saw that they were courteous to you. You will therefore have them as assistants, that you may be the better able to keep his commands: for it is impossible that these commandments can be observed without these virgins. I see, moreover, that they abide with you willingly; but I will also instruct them not to depart at all from your house: do you only keep your house pure, as they will delight to dwell in a pure abode. For they are pure, and chaste, and industrious, and have all influence with the Lord. Therefore, if they find your house to be pure, they will remain with you; but if any defilement, even a little, befall it, they will immediately withdraw from your house. For these virgins do not at all like any defilement.” I said to him, “I hope, sir, that I will please them, so that they may always be willing to inhabit my house. And as he to whom you entrusted me has no complaint against me, so neither will they have.” He said to the Shepherd, “I see that the servant of God wishes to live, and to keep these commandments, and will place these virgins in a pure habitation.” When he had spoken these words he again delivered me to the Shepherd, and called those virgins, and said to them, “Since I see that you are willing to dwell in his house, I commend him and his house to you, asking that you withdraw not at all from it.” And the virgins heard these words with pleasure.

The angel then said to me, “Conduct yourself manfully in this service, and make known to every one the great things of God, and you will have favour in this ministry. Whoever, therefore, shall walk in these commandments, shall have life, and will be happy in his life; but whosoever shall neglect them shall not have life, and will be unhappy in this life. Enjoin all, who are able to act rightly, not to cease well-doing; for, to practise good works is useful to them. And I say that every man ought to be saved from inconveniences. For both he who is in want, and he who suffers inconveniences in his daily life, is in great torture and necessity. Whoever, therefore, rescues a soul of this kind from necessity, will gain for himself great joy. For he who is harassed by inconveniences of this kind, suffers equal torture with him who is in chains. Moreover many, on account of calamities of this sort, when they could not endure them, hasten their own deaths. Whoever, then, knows a calamity of this kind afflicting a man, and does not save him, commits a great sin, and becomes guilty of his blood. Do good works, therefore, ye who have received good from the Lord; lest, while ye delay to do them, the building of the tower be finished, and you be rejected from the edifice: there is now no other tower a-building. For on your account was the work of building suspended. Unless, then, you make haste to do rightly, the tower will be completed, and you will be excluded.”

After he had spoken with me he rose up from the couch, and taking the Shepherd and the virgins, he departed. But he said to me that he would send back the Shepherd and the virgins to my dwelling. Amen.

Eusebius speaks of Papias as a man most learned in all things, and well acquainted with the Scriptures. In another passage he describes him as of small capacity. The fragments of Papias are translated from the text given in Routh’s _Reliquiæ Sacræ_, vol. i.

[The writings of Papias in common circulation are five in number, and these are called an Exposition of the Oracles of the Lord. Irenæus makes mention of these as the only works written by him, in the following words: “Now testimony is borne to these things in writing by Papias, an ancient man, who was a hearer of John, and a friend of Polycarp, in the fourth of his books; for five books were composed by him.” Thus wrote Irenæus. Moreover, Papias himself, in the introduction to his books, makes it manifest that he was not himself a hearer and eye-witness of the holy apostles; but he tells us that he received the truths of our religion from those who were acquainted with them [the apostles] in the following words:]

But I shall not be unwilling to put down, along with my interpretations, whatsoever instructions I received with care at any time from the elders, and stored up with care in my memory, assuring you at the same time of their truth. For I did not, like the multitude, take pleasure in those who spoke much, but in those who taught the truth; nor in those who related strange commandments, but in those who rehearsed the commandments given by the Lord to faith, and proceeding from truth itself. If, then, any one who had attended on the elders came, I asked minutely after their sayings,—what Andrew or Peter said, or what was said by Philip, or by Thomas, or by James, or by John, or by Matthew, or by any other of the Lord’s disciples: which things Aristion and the presbyter John, the disciples of the Lord, say. For I imagined that what was to be got from books was not so profitable to me as what came from the living and abiding voice.

[The early Christians] _called those who practised a godly guilelessness_, _children_, [as is stated by Papias in the first book of the Lord’s Expositions, and by Clemens Alexandrinus in his _Pædagogue_.]

Judas walked about in this world a sad example of impiety; for his body having swollen to such an extent that he could not pass where a chariot could pass easily, he was crushed by the chariot, so that his bowels gushed out.

[As the elders who saw John the disciple of the Lord remembered that they had heard from him how the Lord taught in regard to those times, and said]: “The days will come in which vines shall grow, having each ten thousand branches, and in each branch ten thousand twigs, and in each true twig ten thousand shoots, and in every one of the shoots ten thousand clusters, and on every one of the clusters ten thousand grapes, and every grape when pressed will give five-and-twenty metretes of wine. And when any one of the saints shall lay hold of a cluster, another shall cry out, ‘I am a better cluster, take me; bless the Lord through me.’ In like manner, [He said] that a grain of wheat would produce ten thousand ears, and that every ear would have ten thousand grains, and every grain would yield ten pounds of clear, pure, fine flour; and that apples, and seeds, and grass would produce in similar proportions; and that all animals, feeding then only on the productions of the earth, would become peaceable and harmonious, and be in perfect subjection to man.” [Testimony is borne to these things in writing by Papias, an ancient man, who was a hearer of John and a friend of Polycarp, in the fourth of his books; for five books were composed by him. And he added, saying, “Now these things are credible to believers. And Judas the traitor,” says he, “not believing, and asking, ‘How shall such growths be accomplished by the Lord?’ the Lord said, ‘They shall see who shall come to them.’ These, then, are the times mentioned by the prophet Isaiah: ‘And the wolf shall lie down with the lamb,’ etc. (Isa. xi. 6 ff.).”]

As the presbyters say, then those who are deemed worthy of an abode in heaven shall go there, others shall enjoy the delights of Paradise, and others shall possess the splendour of the city; for everywhere the Saviour will be seen, according as they shall be worthy who see Him. But that there is this distinction between the habitation of those who produce an hundred-fold, and that of those who produce sixty-fold, and that of those who produce thirty-fold; for the first will be taken up into the heavens, the second class will dwell in Paradise, and the last will inhabit the city; and that on this account the Lord said, “In my Father’s house are many mansions:” for all things belong to God, who supplies all with a suitable dwelling-place, even as His word says, that a share is given to all by the Father, according as each one is or shall be worthy. And this is the couch in which they shall recline who feast, being invited to the wedding. The presbyters, the disciples of the apostles, say that this is the gradation and arrangement of those who are saved, and that they advance through steps of this nature; and that, moreover, they ascend through the Spirit to the Son, and through the Son to the Father; and that in due time the Son will yield up His work to the Father, even as it is said by the apostle, “For He must reign till He hath put all enemies under His feet. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.” For in the times of the kingdom the just man who is on the earth shall forget to die. “But when He saith all things are put under Him, it is manifest that He is excepted which did put all things under Him. And when all things shall be subdued unto Him, then shall the Son also Himself be subject unto Him that put all things under Him, that God may be all in all.”

[Papias, who is now mentioned by us, affirms that he received the sayings of the apostles from those who accompanied them, and he moreover asserts that he heard in person Aristion and the presbyter John. Accordingly he mentions them frequently by name, and in his writings gives their traditions. Our notice of these circumstances may not be without its use. It may also be worth while to add to the statements of Papias already given, other passages of his in which he relates some miraculous deeds, stating that he acquired the knowledge of them from tradition. The residence of the Apostle Philip with his daughters in Hierapolis has been mentioned above. We must now point out how Papias, who lived at the same time, relates that he had received a wonderful narrative from the daughters of Philip. For he relates that a dead man was raised to life in his day. He also mentions another miracle relating to Justus, surnamed Barsabas, how he swallowed a deadly poison, and received no harm, on account of the grace of the Lord. The same person, moreover, has set down other things as coming to him from unwritten tradition, amongst these some strange parables and instructions of the Saviour, and some other things of a more fabulous nature. Amongst these he says that there will be a millennium after the resurrection from the dead, when the personal reign of Christ will be established on this earth. He moreover hands down, in his own writing, other narratives given by the previously mentioned Aristion of the Lord’s sayings, and the traditions of the presbyter John. For information on these points, we can merely refer our readers to the books themselves; but now, to the extracts already made, we shall add, as being a matter of primary importance, a tradition regarding Mark who wrote the Gospel, which he [Papias] has given in the following words]: And the presbyter said this. Mark having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately whatsoever he remembered. It was not, however, in exact order that he related the sayings or deeds of Christ. For he neither heard the Lord nor accompanied Him. But afterwards, as I said, he accompanied Peter, who accommodated his instructions to the necessities [of his hearers], but with no intention of giving a regular narrative of the Lord’s sayings. Wherefore Mark made no mistake in thus writing some things as he remembered them. For of one thing he took especial care, not to omit anything he had heard, and not to put anything fictitious into the statements. [This is what is related by Papias regarding Mark; but with regard to Matthew he has made the following statements]: Matthew put together the oracles [of the Lord] in the Hebrew language, and each one interpreted them as best he could. [The same person uses proofs from the First Epistle of John, and from the Epistle of Peter in like manner. And he also gives another story of a woman who was accused of many sins before the Lord, which is to be found in the Gospel according to the Hebrews.]

_Papias thus speaks, word for word_: To some of them [angels] He gave dominion over the arrangement of the world, and He commissioned them to exercise their dominion well. _And he says, immediately after this_: but it happened that their arrangement came to nothing.

With regard to the inspiration of the book (Revelation), we deem it superfluous to add another word; for the blessed Gregory Theologus and Cyril, and even men of still older date, Papias, Irenæus, Methodius, and Hippolytus, bore entirely satisfactory testimony to it.

Taking occasion from Papias of Hierapolis, the illustrious, a disciple of the apostle who leaned on the bosom of Christ, and Clemens, and Pantænus the priest of [the church] of the Alexandrians, and the wise Ammonius, the ancient and first expositors, who agreed with each other, who understood the work of the six days as referring to Christ and the whole church.

(1.) Mary the mother of the Lord; (2.) Mary the wife of Cleophas or Alpheus, who was the mother of James the bishop and apostle, and of Simon and Thaddeus, and of one Joseph; (3.) Mary Salome, wife of Zebedee, mother of John the evangelist and James; (4.) Mary Magdalene. These four are found in the Gospel. James and Judas and Joseph were sons of an aunt (2) of the Lord’s. James also and John were sons of another aunt (3) of the Lord’s. Mary (2), mother of James the less and Joseph, wife of Alpheus, was the sister of Mary the mother of the Lord, whom John names of Cleophas, either from her father or from the family of the clan, or for some other reason. Mary Salome (3) is called Salome either from her husband or her village. Some affirm that she is the same as Mary of Cleophas, because she had two husbands.

**The core cluster: the potter has no noun.** Hebrew has no freestanding word for "potter": the potter is *yotser*, the qal participle of יָצַר *yatsar* (H3335), "the forming one." H3335 occurs 44 times, and Isaiah owns it — 23 of 44 occurrences, with Psalms next at 7, Jeremiah 5, Genesis 3. The gloss range is dominated by participial forms ("the.[one]," "[who].formed," "[is.the.one.who].formed"), which is the finding: God-as-potter and God-as-creator are one word, and whether a translator writes "potter" or "Creator" at any occurrence is a rendering choice, not a lexical one. The corpus tagging makes the same point from the other side: at Jer 18:4 and Ps 2:9 the participle is split out as its own lemma יוֹצֵר H3335a "the.potter," while at Isa 64:7 (MT; English 64:8) the identical participle stays under verb H3335, glossed "[are the.one.who].formed.us" — the same word crossing the potter/Creator line inside one tagging scheme.

**The root's double life.** One step to the noun יֵצֶר H3336 (9x) was the richest neighbor move: its gloss range runs inclination (5 forms), form (2), and — once — "a.pot" (Isa 29:16). The same noun is the evil "inclination" of every thought in Gen 6:5 and 8:21, the "frame" God remembers is dust in Ps 103:14, and the physical pot of Isaiah's polemic. The Talmudic reading of Gen 2:7's doubled yod as the two *yetsarim* is midrash, not philology — but the consonantal fact underneath it is corpus-verified: Gen 2:7 has וַיִּיצֶר (double yod) for the forming of the man, and the control at Gen 2:19 has וַיִּצֶר (single yod) for the forming of the beasts. One further step, H3338 *yetsurim* "members" (Job 17:7, 1x), added little; the chain was ended there per the stopping rule.

**Clay hides behind a homograph.** A bare query on H2563 חֹמֶר returns only the dry-measure *homer* (13x); clay-*chomer* lives under **H2563b** (17x — glossed clay 9, mud 3, mortar 3), and H2563a is a third homograph ("heap," Hab 3:15, 1x). The H2563b distribution is a discovery about ownership: **Job 7, Isaiah 5, Jeremiah 2**. Isaiah owns the potter; *Job owns the clay* — and only in Job does the clay speak in the first person: "Remember that You molded me like clay. Would You now return me to dust?" (10:9); "I was also formed from clay" (33:6, Elihu leveling himself with Job); plus houses of clay (4:19), defenses of clay (13:12), clay under the seal (38:14). The same word is Babel's mortar (Gen 11:3) and Egypt's brick-slavery (Exod 1:14). The other clay words sort by register: חֶרֶשׂ H2789 (17x) is the fired thing — earthenware and potsherd — and Leviticus owns it (5x), always as the vessel that must be *broken* when defiled (Lev 11:33, 15:12); its poetic uses are dryness and fragment (Job 2:8; Ps 22:15 [MT 22:16]). טִיט H2916 (13x) is trodden mire — and Isa 41:25 puts the potter in the conquest register: the one from the north tramples rulers "like a potter who treads the clay." In Aramaic the whole vocabulary belongs to Daniel 2: חֲסַף (H2635, 9x, all Dan 2) with טִין "miry" (H2917), against a single Aramaic potter פֶּחָר (H6353, Dan 2:41). By English gloss, Daniel is the top "clay" book in the whole Bible (17 tokens) — clay there is not creatureliness but the brittleness of empire.

**The Greek side is tiny, and the roles have changed.** κεραμεύς "potter" occurs 3 times: Rom 9:21 and twice in Matt 27, where the potter appears only as the former owner of a field bought with blood money. κεραμικός once (Rev 2:27, quoting Ps 2:9's כְלִי יוֹצֵר shattering). πλάσσω, the LXX's verb for *yatsar*, survives twice (Rom 9:20 "will the thing formed [πλάσμα] say to him who formed it"; 1 Tim 2:13 "Adam was formed first") and ὀστράκινος "earthen" twice (2 Cor 4:7 treasure in clay vessels; 2 Tim 2:20 vessels of honor and dishonor). But πηλός "clay" occurs 6 times, and **five of the six are John 9** — Jesus making mud to open a blind man's eyes. In the NT, God never sits at the wheel: the potter survives only inside quotation and argument, while the one new clay-act in the corpus is remedial, clay applied *to* a man rather than a man made *from* clay. (Reading John 9 as a deliberate echo of Gen 2:7 is patristic tradition, not corpus data; the corpus gives only the shared word.) One more Greek thread is internal to Paul: the "lump" of Rom 9:21 is φύραμα (G5445, 5x), and its other Romans occurrence is 11:16 — "if the firstfruit is holy, so is the lump" — the same lump moving from wrath-and-mercy vessels to consecrated dough within one letter; its remaining uses are all leaven sayings (1 Cor 5:6-7; Gal 5:9).

**Register map.** The image does at least seven different jobs. (1) *Polemic against the questioning creature*: Isa 29:16 ("shall what is formed say of him who formed it, 'He has no understanding'?"), Isa 45:9-11, Rom 9:20-21, Wis 15:7 — and IMITATION.51.5 quotes it straight: "For how shall the clay boast against Him that fashioned it?" (2) *Covenant plasticity*: Jer 18:1-6, the wet-clay oracle — "the vessel... became flawed [וְנִשְׁחַת, niphal of שָׁחַת H7843] in his hand; so he formed it into another vessel." The corpus lemma for "marred" is the destroy/corrupt verb, and the whole point is that at the wheel, marring is not final. (3) *Petition*: Isa 64:8 (MT 64:7) — "we are the clay, and You are the potter" — the only place the clay speaks *as* prayer rather than under rebuke; Job 10:9 is its private twin. Cross-references confirm this verse as the theme's hub (linked by voters to Jer 18, Isa 29:16, 45:9, Rom 9, Ps 119:73, Eph 2:10), and find_similar makes its nearest neighbor Sir 33:13 (0.718). (4) *Shattering of the fired vessel*: Ps 2:9 → Rev 2:26-27; Isa 30:14 (no shard left big enough to scoop coals); Jer 19:11 ("like one shatters a potter's jar that can never again be repaired"); Jer 22:28 (Coniah a despised pot); Lam 4:2 (Zion's sons, gold re-valued as potter's jars); Hos 8:8. Jer 18 and Jer 19 are a staged pair: the same prophet buys wet clay reworked at the wheel, then a fired jar smashed at Topheth — reversibility ends at the kiln. (5) *Frailty holding treasure*: Job 4:19's "houses of clay" (quoted at length in 1CLEMENT.39.1), 2 Cor 4:7, 2 Tim 2:20-21, Ps 22:15's dried potsherd. (6) *Craft and economy*: Sir 38:29-34's potter at his kick-wheel, excluded from council yet "they maintain the fabric of the age; their prayer is in the handiwork of their craft"; the royal potters' guild at Netaim and Gederah (1 Chr 4:23); Leviticus's breakable purity vessels. (7) *The betrayal price*: Zech 11:13's thirty pieces thrown "to the potter" in the LORD's house → Matt 27:7-10. Both named potter-places in the corpus end as graveyards: Topheth (8 mentions, all 2 Kgs 23 + Jer 7 and 19) and Akeldama/potter's field (Matt 27:8; Acts 1:19).

**The Apocrypha is a load-bearing layer here.** Wis 15:7 states Rom 9:21's exact argument a step earlier — one clay, vessels for clean uses and their contrary, "the potter is the judge" — then turns it against the idol-maker: the potter, "having but a little before been made of earth," molds a god from the same clay and must soon "give back the soul which was lent him" (15:8). Sir 33:13 gives the determinist maximum ("as the clay of the potter in his hand... so men are in the hand of him who made them"), immediately after Adam-from-dust (33:10). Sir 27:5 supplies the kiln-test proverb; 2 Esd 8:2 the earth's own economics ("much clay from which earthen vessels are made, but little dust that gold comes from"). That Paul knew Wisdom is standard scholarship, not corpus data — but the verbal skeleton (same clay, two contrary uses, potter as judge) is visible in the corpus text itself.

**The prose classics keep the clay and drop the potter.** Augustine uses the potter's wheel to argue about *time* (CONFESSIONS.11.29 — would the wheel's turning still measure time if the heavens stopped?), and pointedly rejects the artificer analogy for creation: God is not like a human maker who "invests with a form what already existeth... as clay, or stone" (11.7) — ex nihilo against the potter image. Yet the incarnation is "a lowly habitation of our clay" (7.24), and Monica delays his baptism preferring "to expose to them the clay whence I might afterwards be moulded, than the very cast, when made" (1.18). Julian uses clay to mark the body/soul frontier: the body from "the clay of earth," but for the soul God "would take right nought" (JULIAN.62.7). Chesterton's sculptor "is glad that the clay is colourless" — creation loves its limits (ORTHODOXY.3.23). Bunyan has one glancing "vessels of clay" (PILGRIM.1.616). Brother Lawrence (PRESENCE) and Barnabas: zero hits — a genuine layer gap, stated as such.

**Synthesis question.** The corpus leaves one live wire exposed: **can the vessel change its use — is honor assigned at the wheel (Rom 9:21; Sir 33:13; Wis 15:7), or attainable by the vessel's own purging (2 Tim 2:20-21, where "if anyone purges himself he will be a vessel for honor," in the same σκεῦος-εἰς-τιμήν vocabulary), and is Jer 18's re-made pot the potter's prerogative or the nation's repentance (18:8, 18:11)?**

"Shall what is formed say of him who formed it, 'He has no understanding'?" (Isaiah 29:16). Isaiah asks it as a taunt — you have turned things upside down, as though the clay could file a complaint against the potter. Sixteen chapters later, Isaiah 45:9-11 repeats the ban on the questioning creature, and Paul carries it into Greek: "will the thing formed say to him who formed it?" (Romans 9:20). Fourteen centuries after that, Thomas à Kempis is still enforcing it: "For how shall the clay boast against Him that fashioned it?" (Imitation 51.5).

And yet the hub of this whole theme — the verse the cross-reference voters link to Jeremiah 18, Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9, Romans 9, and Psalm 119:73 — is a verse in which the clay speaks. "We are the clay, and You are the potter" (Isaiah 64:8; the Hebrew sits at MT 64:7). Same vocabulary, same two parties, opposite register: not the creature interrogating upward but the creature conceding everything and asking anyway, a petition prayed from inside ruin. Job 10:9 is its private twin — "Remember that You molded me like clay. Would You now return me to dust?" — and the corpus never rebukes either speaker.

So the live tension in this material is not whether God is the potter; everyone in the corpus grants that. It is what the clay is allowed to say — rebuked when it questions, heard when it prays — and, behind that, the harder question the survey leaves exposed at the end: whether the clay is ever allowed to *do* anything.

Hebrew never coined a word for "potter." The potter is *yotser*, the qal participle of יָצַר *yatsar* (H3335), "the forming one" — the same verb that forms the man from dust in Genesis 2:7 and the light in Isaiah 45:7. The verb occurs 44 times, and Isaiah owns it, 23 of the 44. Whether an English Bible prints "potter" or "Creator" at any given occurrence is a rendering choice, not a lexical one, and the corpus tagging betrays the same instability from the inside: at Jeremiah 18:4 and Psalm 2:9 the participle is split out as its own lemma, H3335a "the potter," while the identical participle at Isaiah 64:7 (MT) stays filed under the plain verb, glossed "the one who formed us." One word keeps crossing the potter/Creator line inside a single tagging scheme.

The naming runs in the opposite direction from ours. Greek κεραμεύς is built on κέραμος, potter's earth, fired ware; English "potter" is built on "pot." Those languages name the craftsman from his finished product — the hard thing at the end. Hebrew names him from the act: the wet stage, the hands still on. A language quietly decides which moment of the craft the craftsman *is*, and Hebrew chose the moment when the material can still move.

One step from the verb sits its noun, יֵצֶר *yetser* (H3336), nine occurrences, and it lives a double life: five times "inclination," twice "form," and once — Isaiah 29:16, the taunt verse itself — a physical pot. The same word is the evil inclination of every human thought in Genesis 6:5 and the frame God remembers is dust in Psalm 103:14: what a person is shaped *from* and what a person is shaped *toward*, sharing one noun. The Talmudic reading of Genesis 2:7's doubled yod as the two *yetsarim*, the good and evil inclinations, is midrash, not philology — but the consonantal fact underneath it is corpus-verified: the forming of the man carries וַיִּיצֶר with two yods, and the control verse, the forming of the beasts at 2:19, carries only one.

The synagogue eventually welded the two nouns into a single sentence. The piyyut *Ki Hinei Kachomer*, sung as Yom Kippur begins, sets Jeremiah's image — "as clay in the hand of the potter, who widens or contracts it at will, so are we in Your hand" — against the refrain "look to the covenant, and do not regard the *yetser*." Clay and inclination, H2563b and H3336, in one breath: remake the material, the liturgy asks, and overlook what it keeps inclining toward. That is outside this corpus, but it is the corpus's own two nouns doing the work.

The Hebrew for the potter's clay hides behind a homograph. Bare חֹמֶר (H2563) is a dry measure, the homer; clay-*chomer* is filed at H2563b, seventeen occurrences — and their distribution is a finding about ownership: Job seven, Isaiah five, Jeremiah two. Isaiah owns the potter; *Job owns the clay*. Only in Job does the clay speak in the first person — 10:9 above, and Elihu leveling himself at 33:6, "I was also formed from clay." The same word is Babel's mortar (Genesis 11:3) and Egypt's brick-slavery (Exodus 1:14): building material for empires, body material for one scraped man on an ash heap.

The other clay words sort by register. חֶרֶשׂ (H2789) is the fired thing, earthenware and potsherd, and Leviticus owns it — always as the vessel that must be *broken* when defiled (Leviticus 11:33, 15:12), never washed. טִיט (H2916) is trodden mire: Isaiah 41:25 puts the potter in the conquest register, the one from the north trampling rulers "like a potter who treads the clay" — and Jeremiah, the corpus's one potter-watching prophet, ends up sunk in that same word at the bottom of a cistern (Jeremiah 38:6). And in Aramaic the whole vocabulary belongs to Daniel 2: חֲסַף, nine occurrences, every one of them in the statue vision, with a single Aramaic potter (Daniel 2:41). Counted by English gloss Daniel is the top "clay" book in the Bible, seventeen tokens — though the survey flags six of those as a tokenization artifact, a stray Aramaic determiner swept in as a clay-gloss carrier. Even corrected, the point stands: in Daniel clay is not creatureliness but the brittleness of empire, iron and clay that "will not adhere to one another."

Jeremiah 18 and 19 are a staged pair, and everything turns on what state the clay is in. In chapter 18 the prophet watches wet clay at the wheel: "the vessel... became flawed in his hand; so he formed it into another vessel." The corpus lemma under "flawed" is the heavy one — נִשְׁחַת, niphal of שָׁחַת (H7843), the corrupt/destroy verb, and the link the survey flagged is now tool-verified: Genesis 6:12 carries the same lemma twice of the flood-ruined earth ("it was corrupt... all flesh had corrupted its way"). The grammar is making Jeremiah's point for him: the vessel on the wheel is described with the vocabulary of the flood — and reworked anyway. At the wheel, even *destroyed* is a provisional state. In chapter 19 the same prophet buys a *fired* jar and smashes it at Topheth: "like one shatters a potter's jar that can never again be repaired."

The line between the two chapters is a real threshold in the material. Wet clay owes its reworkability to films of water between mineral plates; even bone-dry unfired clay can be slaked back to plasticity with water. But fire the piece past roughly 500 °C and the clay minerals surrender their chemically bound water — dehydroxylation — and no amount of soaking ever restores the plastic state. Reversibility does not fade gradually; it ends at the kiln, which is exactly where Jeremiah staged its ending. Sirach knew the kiln as the moment of judgment from the craft side: the furnace is where the potter's vessels are proved (Sirach 27:5).

Two footnotes from the potter's yard sharpen the oracle rather than softening it. First: fired clay is not actually useless — potters have always ground broken sherds into grog and kneaded it into fresh clay as temper. What the kiln makes irreversible is not the *stuff* but the *vessel*; the material survives, the form does not. Jeremiah 19 aims precisely at the form: a jar, never again repaired. Lamentations 4:2 runs the same devaluation in one line — Zion's sons, once fine gold, now reckoned as potter's jars. Second: the sherd had an afterlife the oracles don't mention. Broken pottery was the ancient scrap paper, and the ostraca from Lachish — Hebrew military dispatches inked on potsherds during the very Babylonian campaign Jeremiah preached through — are among the last written words of the kingdom the smashed jar stood for. Isaiah 30:14 promises a shattering so total no shard remains big enough to scoop coals; it is shards that carried the archive out.

Cross into Greek and the potter has almost vanished. κεραμεύς occurs three times: once in Romans 9:21, twice in Matthew 27 — where the potter is no maker at all, merely the former owner of a field bought with betrayal money, closing the loop from Zechariah 11:13's thirty pieces thrown "to the potter" in the LORD's house. (Training knowledge says the LXX reads "foundry" there and the Syriac "treasury" against the MT's "potter" — but this corpus carries no LXX layer to check it, so that stays a flag, not a fact.) Both named potter-places in the corpus end as graveyards: Topheth, and Akeldama, the field of blood. In the New Testament God never once sits at the wheel; the potter survives only inside quotation (Revelation 2:27's κεραμικός, riding the Psalm 2:9 line about shattering the nations like a *yotser's* vessel) and inside argument (Romans 9).

Meanwhile the one genuinely new clay-act in the whole corpus runs the image backward. πηλός, "clay," occurs six times in the New Testament, and five of them are John 9: Jesus spitting, kneading mud, spreading it on a blind man's eyes. Spittle-cures were a recognized healing gesture in that world — Tacitus has Vespasian curing a blind man with spittle at Alexandria — but the *clay* is John's addition, and it is remedial: clay applied *to* a man, not a man made *from* clay. Reading the scene as a deliberate echo of Genesis 2:7, the Creator resuming hand-work on unfinished eyes, is patristic tradition, not corpus data; the corpus supplies only the shared word, and the reversal of direction.

Paul, for his part, lets the lump escape the argument it was made for. The "lump" of Romans 9:21 is φύραμα, and its only other occurrence in Romans is 11:16 — "if the firstfruit is holy, so is the lump." Within one letter the same word moves from the wheel, where vessels of wrath and mercy are decreed, to the kitchen, where holiness spreads through dough. And behind Romans 9 stands the Wisdom of Solomon, which states the argument a step earlier — one clay, vessels for clean uses and their contraries, "the potter is the judge" (Wisdom 15:7) — then swings it against the idol-maker: the potter, himself "but a little before... made of earth," molds a god from the same clay and must soon give back the soul which was lent him. That Paul knew Wisdom is standard scholarship, not corpus data; but the verbal skeleton — same clay, two contrary uses, potter as judge — is visible in the corpus text itself. Sirach holds down the determinist maximum ("as the clay of the potter in his hand... so men are in the hand of him who made them," 33:13, placed straight after Adam-from-dust) — and also the craft's dignity: the potter at his kick-wheel, excluded from the council, yet of him and his fellow artisans, "they maintain the fabric of the age; their prayer is in the handiwork of their craft" (38:29-34).

The prose classics complete the attrition: they keep the clay and drop the potter. Augustine rejects the artificer analogy outright — God is not like a human maker who "invests with a form what already existeth... as clay, or stone" (Confessions 11.7); creation from nothing has no wheel and no prior lump. Yet he cannot do without the material: the incarnation is "a lowly habitation of our clay" (7.24), and Monica delays his baptism preferring "to expose to them the clay whence I might afterwards be moulded, than the very cast, when made" (1.18) — wet-state theology in a mother's decision. And the wheel itself returns in Augustine for one last job, arguing about *time*: if the heavenly bodies stood still and a potter's wheel kept turning, would its turning not still measure time (11.29)? Time, he concludes, is not the motion of the heavens. Sixteen centuries later metrology conceded the point: since 1967 the second has been defined not by any celestial motion but by 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a cesium-133 atom — timekeeping formally detached from the heavens and handed to the humbler motions of matter. The potter's wheel was always a good enough clock.

Julian of Norwich uses clay to draw the body/soul frontier — the body from "the clay of earth," but for the soul God "would take right nought" (62.7). Chesterton's sculptor "is glad that the clay is colourless": creation loving its limits (Orthodoxy 3.23). Clement of Rome quotes Job's "houses of clay" at length (1 Clement 39.1). And Brother Lawrence and Barnabas contain no potter and no clay at all — a genuine thin layer, logged as such; the theme's prose weight sits almost entirely in Augustine and à Kempis.

The survey leaves one wire exposed, and this piece will not insulate it. Is the vessel's use assigned at the wheel — the potter making from one lump a vessel for honor and one for dishonor (Romans 9:21), men in the hand of their maker as clay in the potter's (Sirach 33:13), the potter as judge (Wisdom 15:7)? Or can the vessel change its own use — "if anyone purges himself, he will be a vessel for honor" (2 Timothy 2:21), in the very σκεῦος-εἰς-τιμήν vocabulary of Romans 9? Jeremiah 18 sits on both sides at once: the reforming of the marred pot is entirely the potter's act at the wheel — and yet the oracle's application turns and commands the nation to repent (18:8, 18:11), as though the clay's turning and the potter's re-turning were somehow one motion.

The corpus rebukes the clay that questions and answers the clay that prays. It never says which of those the purged vessel is doing. What is the clay allowed to say — and has anything it said ever turned the wheel?

Training-knowledge welds not checkable against this corpus; these rest on the model's confidence and should be editor-reviewed, not tool-verified:

Etymology: Greek κεραμεύς is derived from κέραμος (potter's earth / fired ware); English "potter" from "pot." The contrast with the Hebrew participle's act-naming is the weld. - Ceramics chemistry: unfired clay (even bone-dry greenware) can be slaked back to plastic clay with water; firing past roughly 450-600 °C drives off chemically bound hydroxyl water (dehydroxylation of clay minerals such as kaolinite), after which plasticity is unrecoverable. - Grog: crushed fired sherds are kneaded into fresh clay as temper, a practice attested in ancient wares (grog-tempered pottery). - Lachish ostraca: Hebrew military dispatches written on potsherds during the final Babylonian campaign against Judah (c. 589-586 BC). - *Ki Hinei Kachomer*: piyyut sung at the start of Yom Kippur; stanza "like clay in the hand of the potter" with the refrain "look to the covenant, and do not regard the *yetser*." - Tacitus, *Histories* 4.81: Vespasian at Alexandria heals a blind man using spittle. - SI second: redefined in 1967 as 9,192,631,770 periods of the cesium-133 hyperfine transition, replacing astronomical definitions. - Inherited flag (survey claim 10): LXX Zech 11:13 "foundry/furnace" and Syriac "treasury" against MT "potter" — asserted here only as an unverifiable training-knowledge note; both corpus translations read "potter" and no LXX layer exists to check.

**The phrase and its camouflage.** The exact phrase "living water" occurs only 7 times in a BSB full-text search: John 7:38; John 4:10, 11; Jer 2:13; Jer 17:13; Zech 14:8; Rev 7:17. But the Hebrew phrase *mayim chayyim* (H4325 + H2416a) is wider than English lets on. Interlinear checks confirm the identical construction — noun *mayim* + adjective *chayyim* (parsed Aampa, "living") — at Gen 26:19 (BSB "a well of **flowing** water"), Lev 14:5-6 (BSB "**running** water" / "the **fresh** water"), Num 19:17 (BSB "**fresh** water"), and Song 4:15 (BSB "a well of **fresh** water"). The corpus data thus shows the English translation itself performing a register split the Hebrew does not make: where the water is ritual or erotic, translators write "fresh/running"; where it is theological, they write "living." A keyword survey of the English text silently loses the ritual half of the theme. That is a finding about method as much as about the theme.

**Who owns the words.** *Mayim* is huge and evenly spread — 581 occurrences, led by Isaiah (56), Genesis (54), Psalms (53). The discriminating words are the source-nouns. *Maqor* ("fountain/spring," H4726) occurs only 18 times, and Proverbs owns it (7), followed by Jeremiah (4), Leviticus (3). Its first canonical appearances are gynecological: Lev 12:7 and 20:18 use *maqor* for "the source of her blood" — the fountain is first a woman's body, only later a metaphor for God (that sequencing is corpus data; what to make of it is inference). *Ma'yan* ("spring," H4599, 23x) opens cosmically — the "fountains of the great deep" of the flood (Gen 7:11; 8:2) — and closes doxologically ("all my springs are in you," Ps 87:7). *Be'er* ("well," H0875, 37x) belongs to Genesis (23 of 37): dug, named, quarreled over. *Bor* ("cistern," H0953) skews to Jeremiah (13 of 26 hits on the gloss "cistern"), where it is both his metaphor (2:13) and his prison (38:6-13) — the prophet of the broken cisterns is himself lowered into one. On the Greek side, *hydōr* (G5204, 79x) is majority-owned by two books: John (24) and Revelation (18) — more than half the NT's water is Johannine. *Pēgē* (G4077) is only 11x: Rev 5, John 3. *Potamos* (G4215, 17x): Rev 8. The NT theme is not diffuse; it is a Johannine possession.

**The grammatical fault line in the Greek.** John's Gospel uses the participle: *hydōr zōn* (John 4:10, ASN participle of *zaō*; genitive *hydatos zōntos* in 7:38) — a direct calque of *mayim chayyim*, water that is itself alive. Revelation never does. Interlinear checks show Rev 7:17 has *zōēs pēgas hydatōn* ("fountains of waters **of life**," noun genitive), and Rev 21:6 and 22:1, 17 likewise use *hydōr zōēs*, "water of life." BSB's "springs of living water" at Rev 7:17 hides this. The participle (water that lives) is confined to Jeremiah's Hebrew, Zechariah, and Jesus's two dialogues; the Apocalypse converts it to a genitive of what the water gives. Whether that shift is theologically loaded is inference; that it is total within the corpus is data.

**Register map.** The same phrase does at least seven different jobs: - *Property dispute* — Gen 26:19: Isaac's servants dig and find *be'er mayim chayyim*; the herdsmen of Gerar immediately claim it ("The water is ours!"). Living water enters the canon as contested ground. - *Ritual solvent* — Lev 14:5-6 (cleansing the leper: a bird killed in an earthen vessel *over living water*), Num 19:17 (living water poured over the ashes of the red heifer, the cure for corpse-impurity). In the Torah's cult, living water is the liquid that dissolves death-contact. No metaphor; a recipe. - *Love lyric* — Song 4:15: the bride is "a garden spring, a well of living water, flowing streams from Lebanon." - *Covenant lawsuit* — Jer 2:13: "two evils: they have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves cisterns — broken cisterns that cannot hold water." Echoed as courtroom shame in Jer 17:13. - *Eschatological geography* — Zech 14:8 (living waters out from Jerusalem to both seas, "in summer and in winter" — a spring that does not fail in the dry season, which is the point of *chayyim* here); Ezek 47, where the phrase is absent but the verb saturates: "wherever the river flows... swarms of living creatures... everything will live" (47:9). - *Offer* — John 4:10 ("If you knew the gift [*dōrean*, G1431] of God... He would have given you living water") and the festival shout of John 7:37-38, with the narrator's flat gloss: "He said this about the Spirit" (7:39). The lawsuit's forsaken fountain becomes a thing asked for over a well-curb. - *Consummation* — Rev 7:17 (the Lamb as shepherd leading to the springs), 21:6 and 22:17 (given "freely" to the thirsty), 22:1 (the river from the throne). The community's own cross-reference data ties these tightly back to Jer 2:13 (top votes: John 4:14, John 7:37, Jer 17:13, Rev 21:6, Ps 36:9).

**The wisdom transposition.** Proverbs uses "fountain of life" (*meqor chayyim*) as a transferable predicate: the mouth of the righteous (10:11), the teaching of the wise (13:14), the fear of YHWH (14:27), understanding (16:22) — and Ps 36:9 gives the un-transposed original: "with **You** is the fountain of life." The Apocrypha runs hard down this track. Sir 15:3: wisdom "will give him water of wisdom to drink." Sir 24:25-31: wisdom is Pishon, Tigris, Euphrates, Jordan, Gihon — Eden's whole river system — and the teacher says "I came out as a canal stream from a river... and my stream became a river, and my river became a sea." Bar 3:12 is Jer 2:13 transposed wholesale into the wisdom key: "You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom." And Sir 24:21 states the exact antithesis of John 4:14: "Those who drink me will be **thirsty for more**," against "whoever drinks the water I give him will **never thirst**." Whether John 4:14 is a deliberate reversal of Sirach is standard-scholarship territory (often argued, not provable from this corpus); that the two sentences contradict verbatim is corpus data.

**Where the fountain lives.** Tracking the source's address across the corpus: in Jeremiah the fountain is God, and sin is leaving it for self-dug containers. In John 4:14 the fountain migrates: the water "will become **in him** a fount of water springing up to eternal life"; in John 7:38 "out of his belly will flow rivers." In Revelation the spring is back at the throne, and the believer is a drinker again ("let the one who is thirsty come," 22:17). The drinker becomes a source and then, at the end, a guest. Alongside this runs the thirst question: John 4:14 promises "never thirst"; Sir 24:21 promises "thirsty for more"; Julian says even God thirsts until Doomsday; Ps 42:2 and 63:1 make thirst itself the mark of the living ("my soul thirsts for God, the **living** God" — the adjective migrating from the water to its giver).

**Synthesis question.** Does living water end thirst or teach it — is the corpus's promise satisfaction (John 4:14, Rev 21:6) or the transformation of the drinker into a spring who, like her Source, now thirsts (John 7:38, Sir 24:21, Julian 40)?

Start with what the phrase means when nobody is preaching. In Hebrew, *mayim chayyim* — "living water" — is first a plain description of water that moves: a spring, a running stream, water not drawn and stored but arriving under its own pressure. The survey caught the English text hiding exactly this. The identical construction (noun *mayim* + the adjective *chayyim*, parsed "living") sits at Gen 26:19, Lev 14:5-6, Num 19:17, and Song 4:15 — but wherever the water is a well being dug, a leper being cleansed, or a bride being praised, translators write "flowing," "running," "fresh," and reserve "living" for the theological verses. The register split is the translators', not the Hebrew's. A keyword survey of the English silently loses the ritual half of the theme. That is a finding about method before it is one about God.

And it is a legal finding. In later halakhah — this is training knowledge, not the corpus — *mayim chayyim* is a category with a spec: flowing spring water, undrawn, ranked at the top of the Mishnah's grades of purifying water. When Lev 14 kills a bird over living water and Num 19 pours living water over the ashes of the red heifer, "living" is not poetry. It is the requirement that the water be in motion, because motionless water cannot dissolve death-contact. Living water is the Torah's solvent for corpses.

The theme is carried less by *mayim* — huge and evenly spread, 581 occurrences — than by the rarer source-nouns, and each has a home. *Maqor*, "fountain," appears only 18 times and Proverbs owns seven of them; its first canonical uses (Lev 12:7; 20:18) are gynecological, the "source" of a woman's blood, so the fountain is a body before it is a figure for God. That sequencing is corpus data; what to make of it is inference. *Bor*, "cistern," skews hard to Jeremiah — who is himself lowered into one (38:6). On the Greek side, *hydōr* runs to 79 uses and two books hold most of them: John (24) and Revelation (18). More than half of the New Testament's water is Johannine. The theme is not diffuse; it is a possession.

Jeremiah's indictment is the corpus's sharpest sentence: "My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves cisterns — broken cisterns that cannot hold water" (Jer 2:13). Read as hydrology it is exact, not merely vivid. A Judahite cistern was hewn into limestone and lime-plastered to hold winter rain; when the plaster cracks, it leaks, and the water it does keep goes still and stagnant. A spring needs no plaster and cannot go stale, because it is always leaving. The prophet is not contrasting a good container with a bad one. He is contrasting water that moves with water that is stored — the living with the dead — and choosing the dead. The metaphor of section 1 has become an accusation, and it keeps the physics.

There is a fault line inside the Greek that the English seals over. John's Jesus uses a participle: *hydōr zōn*, water that is itself alive (John 4:10; genitive *hydatos zōntos*, 7:38) — a direct calque of *mayim chayyim*. Revelation never does. It writes *hydōr zōēs*, "water of life" (21:6; 22:1, 17), and "fountains of waters of life" at 7:17, where BSB's "springs of living water" quietly hides the shift. Grammatically the difference is clean: the participle predicates a property intrinsic to the water — it lives — while the genitive names what the water produces — it gives life. That the shift is theologically loaded is inference; that it is total within the corpus is data. The participle (water that lives) belongs to Jeremiah's Hebrew, to Zechariah, and to Jesus's two conversations. The Apocalypse has converted the property into a gift.

The same words work at least seven trades. Living water enters the canon as *contested ground* — Isaac's servants dig a well of it and the herdsmen of Gerar seize it, "The water is ours" (Gen 26:19). It is a *ritual solvent* (Lev 14; Num 19), a *love lyric* (the bride is "a well of living water," Song 4:15), a *covenant lawsuit* (Jer 2:13), an *offer* made over a well-curb ("the gift of God... He would have given you living water," John 4:10), and a *consummation* at the throne (Rev 22:1). Between them stands the *eschatological geography* of Zech 14:8: living waters going out from Jerusalem to both seas, "in summer and in winter." The seasonal clause is the whole point of *chayyim* there, and again it is hydrology. In a karst limestone country almost every wadi is intermittent, running only with the winter rains; a perennial spring like Gihon, which does not fail in the dry months, is rare and precious. "Living" water is water that keeps flowing when everything around it has quit. Never-failing is not a bonus attribute. It is the definition.

Wisdom literature makes "fountain of life" a transferable predicate — the mouth of the righteous (Prov 10:11), the teaching of the wise (13:14), the fear of the LORD (14:27) — while Ps 36:9 keeps the original address: "with **You** is the fountain of life." Then the Apocrypha does something the survey rightly flags. Ben Sira has Wisdom say of those who feed on her, "Those who drink me will be thirsty for more" (Sir 24:21) — the verbatim antithesis of "whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst" (John 4:14). Whether John is deliberately reversing Sirach is standard-scholarship territory, often argued and not provable from this corpus; that the two sentences contradict word for word is corpus data. Baruch, meanwhile, transposes Jeremiah's charge wholesale into the wisdom key: "You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom" (Bar 3:12). The theme has split into two promises that cannot both be simple.

The corpus offers two puns the tools cannot fully settle, and the discipline is to report them as what they are. First: in the Jer 2:13 interlinear, "cisterns" is spelled with an aleph, בֹּארֹת, where Deut 6:11's plain בֹרֹת has none — so the cistern-word takes on the shape of the well-word (*be'er*) at the very moment the verse sets cistern against fountain. That the consonantal difference is really there, the corpus shows; that it is a scribal pun is midrash, not grammar. Second: Jer 17:13 opens "O *miqweh* of Israel," a word the tools gloss only as "hope." But *miqweh* is also the biblical word for a gathering of waters (Gen 1:10) — the root behind the ritual bath, which itself must be filled with living water. If that homograph is in play, the verse reads "O Pool of Israel... they have forsaken the fountain of living water," a sustained water-pun with the theme's own vocabulary. The lexicon returned only "hope," so the water-sense is presumably tagged under a variant Strong's number; this is flagged below as a checkable claim, not asserted.

Outside scripture the theme keeps flowing and keeps arguing with itself. Barnabas 11.1 is an explicit baptismal typology, quoting Jer 2:13's broken cisterns and Ezekiel's river of trees to say "we go down into the water full of sins, and come up bearing fruit" — though the citation index returns *no patristic citations* for Jer 2:13, a real quotation the footnote pipeline missed (logged as a gap). Augustine returns to Ps 36:9 like a refrain and, of his own drought, says "my soul is like a land where no water is" (Conf. 13.19). The *Imitation* makes the fountain Eucharistic and then miniature: barred from the full spring, "yet will I set my lips to the mouth of the heavenly conduit, that at least I may receive a small drop... that I dry not up within my heart" (100.5). Bunyan gives the pilgrims two rivers — the river of the water of life they walk beside, and the bridgeless death-river whose depth varies with their faith (1.929-936). And Julian of Norwich inverts the current entirely: Christ's "I thirst" opens "a property in God of thirst and longing... ever He draweth and drinketh, and yet He thirsteth and longeth" (40.7). In Julian, the fountain is the one who is thirsty.

Track the source's address across the corpus and it will not hold still. In Jeremiah the fountain is God, and sin is leaving him for self-dug tanks. In John 4:14 it migrates inward: the water "will become in him a fountain springing up to eternal life," and by 7:38, "out of his belly will flow rivers." In Revelation the spring is back at the throne and the believer is a drinker again — "let the one who is thirsty come" (22:17). The drinker becomes a source and then, at the last, a guest. Running alongside is the adjective itself, migrating from the water to the one who wants it: "my soul thirsts for God, the **living** God" (Ps 42:2; 63:1). Thirst, here, is not the disease. It is the pulse.

Which is why the survey's question will not close. Physiology says something exact to it, and it does not take John's side. Thirst is not a warning that fires only in emergency; it is a homeostatic signal governed by osmoreceptors that read the blood minute to minute, and drinking quiets it within moments — through the mouth and throat, before a drop has reached the bloodstream — so that satiety is transient by design and recurrence is the sign of a working body. The pathological state is the opposite one: *adipsia*, the loss of thirst, which follows injury to the very centers that generate it. To never thirst again is, in the body's own terms, nearer to a lesion than to a gift.

So the corpus hands its promise forward in two irreconcilable shapes, and the physiology refuses to break the tie. Living water is water that moves; a spring that stopped leaving would be a cistern. Perhaps the drinker who is made into a spring is made, necessarily, into someone who — like the Source that draws and drinks and still thirsts until Doomsday — goes on wanting. Does living water end thirst or teach it?
